chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
title: Staying with Luis Russell and finding a room
summary: Russell's wife had him move out after late nights on 52nd Street; he found a room on 149th Street.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Let’s talk about that trip to New York. So here you’re going down to play with Luis Russell. What happens? You got to get a place to stay. You’re going to New York.

No, Luis Russell told me I could stay at his house until I got situated, until his wife practically told me, you’ve got to get your own room now, because I was going to 52nd Street the nights we weren’t working, coming back in at 5 o-clock in the morning, and I was living – staying in the living room. You know what I mean? Sleeping all day. So that didn’t look – this young boy from Boston.
So where did you finally end up living?
One day, he says his wife had the a-s-s. So he says to me, “You better go to the Y, get you a room.” I was really not Y[MCA] material. I don’t know if I like the Y. So I

was walking from – he lived at 159th Street and Broadway, one of the slick, tall buildings. So I’m walking from there to the Y, which is 135th Street. En route there, I meet this piano player whom I had played with in Connecticut, where I met Charlie Holmes on that gig. He says, “My landlady has a room.” I went over there. It was a brownstone on 149th Street between Amsterdam and Broadway, which in those days was a very nice neighborhood. Still pretty good now. I had a door there for – it was about $5 a week. It had a fireplace and everything in it, really. It was wild. It was a wild period.
